repos.title: Making Images Real Again: A Comprehensive Survey on Deep Image Composition
repos.paper_summary:
This paper surveys deep image composition, a task that combines foreground and background images to produce realistic composites. It decomposes the problem into sub-tasks: object placement, image blending, image harmonization, shadow generation, reflection generation, and generative composition. The authors categorize methods for each sub-task into traditional rule-based approaches and deep learning techniques, such as GANs and diffusion models. They also summarize available datasets and evaluation metrics, including FID, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and user studies.

The paper releases `libcom`, a Python toolbox assembling over 10 functions for these tasks, and an online workbench. Experimental comparisons are provided on specific datasets like OPA (73,470 images) for object placement and iHarmony4 for harmonization. For instance, in object placement, discriminative approaches like FOPA outperform generative ones like PlaceNet. In painterly harmonization, diffusion-based methods like PHDiffusion outperform GAN-based baselines on challenging textures. Limitations include the high cost of collecting paired ground-truth data for harmonization and the difficulty of evaluating arbitrary compositions without dense annotations.

repos.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
repos.paper_summary: AIPOCH Open-Science is an open-source AI research workbench that exports and imports research sessions as portable `.science` packages. The package keeps recorded relations among task context, executed activities, artifact versions, reviews and retained files, and it maps identifiers to the receiving workspace. The authors specify this exchange contract and test it on one controlled session with an incorrect first output, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted permutation test. Complete and partial exports were compared with source snapshots extracted independently of the exporter, and both imports into separate projects retained the tested version and review associations. The unreviewed revision stayed distinct from earlier assessments, and excluded content was marked unavailable. A separate registry case linked a table to its recorded task, execution and review. Offline re-execution of its retained script on a fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. Limitations stated by the paper include that the controlled test used one session and one installation, that native input-edge rows were absent, and that initial task attribution still depends on the surrounding conversation.

digest_headlines.heading: Author affiliations
digest_headlines.headline: The author list spans many hospitals and companies, mainly in China, with affiliations also in the Netherlands, Israel and the United States.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sharing AI-assisted research needs its task, version and review relations to survive transfer, not only the output files.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier provenance and session-sharing systems cover parts of the problem; this work focuses on version and review attribution after exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods and implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The method maps workbench records into typed objects and relations, then checks an exported package against an independently extracted source reference.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Relations, not just files, survived export in a controlled session, with all paired comparisons matching in both exchange conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A failed assessment, its correction and an unreviewed revision can all be true together, so exchange must keep each target separate.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The contract keeps recorded version and review relations across identifier mapping and explicit omissions, with evidence limited to the tested records.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The software is released under Apache 2.0, and a de-identified validation release on Hugging Face contains the protocol, packages and audit scripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of AI assistance
digest_headlines.headline: Codex assisted with literature retrieval, source inspection, application operation and validation code, and the authors remain responsible for interpretation.

digest_headlines.heading: Supplementary Information
digest_headlines.headline: The supplementary figure lists case16 evidence associations and an offline re-execution that reproduced two saved tables byte for byte.

repos.title: KVMem: Virtualizing Million-Token Agent Workspaces on a Consumer GPU
repos.paper_summary:
KVMem is a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed agent workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe. Instead of compacting older context into lossy text summaries or retrieving it as text for repeated prefill, KVMem materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model’s native context window. It uses step-level memory scheduling to update the historical working set once per agent step, query-conditioned retrieval via compact Mean-K indexes derived from the serving model’s attention space, and tiered KV management with position-consistent re-RoPE to restore selected blocks efficiently.

On LongMemEval-S, MemoryAgentBench, and AgentLongBench, KVMem generally achieves higher task utility than compaction-based approaches and reduces post-compaction recovery latency by 11.4–53.8× compared to Compact+RAG. In a DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, KVMem improves task success from 43.8% to 48.4%. On a consumer laptop with a 24 GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU, KVMem supports a 1M-token virtual workspace—four times the model’s 256K-token context window—while sustaining approximately 50 tokens/s in single-session generation. Limitations include the fact that reused KV state is not mathematically equivalent to recomputing text under new contexts, and that retrieval may miss task-relevant blocks if the active execution view is too small.

repos.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
repos.paper_summary:
AutoGen is an open-source framework for building LLM applications via multi-agent conversations. The system defines two core concepts: conversable agents, which are customizable entities backed by LLMs, tools, or human inputs, and conversation programming, a method that structures application logic around inter-agent message passing and control flow. Agents use unified interfaces to send messages and generate replies, with an auto-reply mechanism driving the workflow without a central controller. Developers can program interaction patterns using Python code or natural language instructions embedded in agent prompts.

The paper evaluates AutoGen across six domains. On the MATH dataset (5000 problems), the default two-agent configuration achieved 69.48% accuracy, outperforming vanilla GPT-4 at 55.18%. In ALFWorld decision-making tasks, adding a "grounding" agent improved performance by 15% over a ReAct baseline. For coding tasks on OptiGuide, a multi-agent design increased the F-1 score for identifying unsafe code by 8% with GPT-4 and 35% with GPT-3.5-turbo compared to a single-agent setup. The framework reduced the core workflow code for one application from 430 lines to 100 lines. Limitations include the reliance on proprietary models like GPT-4 for peak performance and the lack of formal safety guarantees for fully autonomous agent interactions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-agent conversation is proposed as the basis for building LLM applications, implemented in the AutoGen framework.

digest_headlines.heading: The AutoGen Framework
digest_headlines.headline: AutoGen rests on conversable agents and conversation programming, where agents exchange messages and control flow emerges from those conversations.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications of AutoGen
digest_headlines.headline: Six example applications test AutoGen across math, retrieval, decision making, coding, group chat and chess.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The discussion frames AutoGen as a general framework and states that its experiments are early, with safety questions left open.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics statement
digest_headlines.headline: The ethics statement names privacy, bias, accountability, trust and unintended consequences as risks to address.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work with a comparison table, expanded discussion, usage guidelines, future work, and supporting figures.

repos.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
repos.paper_summary: OpenVLHarness is a multimodal tool-use harness for MLLMs, built around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer wraps heterogeneous perception, search, and computation tools behind task-level interfaces and renders their outputs into model-readable observations. Memory registers images, structured data, and web references under handles, and a Python Coding Agent runs generated programs over stored values, so later steps can reuse earlier evidence. The harness is evaluated on 22 benchmarks across four domains with eight backbones. Averaged over the 22 datasets, it raises Qwen3-VL-8B from 34.2 to 45.4 and Qwen3-VL-32B from 38.3 to 50.9, outperforming OctoTools and Visual Sketchpad. With GPT-6 Luna at medium effort, it scores 56.5 against 45.8 for the base model, and it is reported to outperform Codex and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort while using at most 37% of their model-token cost. Qwen3-VL results are means of three seeds; GPT-6 results are single runs, so their variance is unreported in the main table. The paper's benchmark-level gains are uneven, with some datasets, such as V* for Qwen3-VL-8B, showing no gain.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Extra reasoning budget gives diminishing returns, so the paper proposes OpenVLHarness to add multimodal evidence acquisition.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness Design
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness pairs a capability layer that renders tool outputs with persistent memory of handle-addressed artifacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness raises Qwen3-VL-8B scores on 22 benchmarks, for example from 32.00 to 48.56 on a counting benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior visual tool-use systems use fixed plans or task-specific frameworks, while this paper keeps multimodal artifacts addressable across turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Released harness gives broad gains on 22 benchmarks and can specialize to domains without updating model weights.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix reports tool-call volume, capability distribution, paired accuracy effects, and object-count distributions of benchmarks.

repos.title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
repos.paper_summary: TailSteer is a final-stage training framework that reduces cumulative drift in multi-turn image editing by steering only the late denoising steps of a base editor. The refined model is trained on its own on-policy rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference, so no curated ground-truth editing pairs are needed. Early steps are trained to match the frozen base model's velocity. Later steps blend that velocity with a preservation velocity toward a source-based endpoint, with the blend weight falling from 1 at the steering onset to 0 at the final step. The method is tested on FLUX.1 Kontext [dev], FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT, and Qwen-Image-2.1. The paper reports substantially reduced drift over 15 to 20 editing turns. On FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, Qwen-IB EN changes by at most +0.47 across the tested steering onsets. Limitations: drift is measured only over 15 to 20 turns, training uses only identity and local edit families, and qualitative comparisons use one steering onset.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: One-shot editors accumulate small errors across repeated turns, so strong single-turn editing does not guarantee long-horizon editing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior fixes add modules, change representations, or add memory, whereas TailSteer trains the base model's own denoising dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: TailSteer trains a copy of the base model on its own rollouts, steering only late denoising steps toward source-preserving endpoints.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across four backbones, TailSteer reduces drift over 15–20 editing turns while keeping single-turn scores close to base models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion says TailSteer reduces cumulative drift across FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen while largely retaining base generative capabilities.

repos.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
repos.paper_summary:
Graph RAG is a method for answering global questions over large text corpora by using an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph and pre-generate hierarchical community summaries. The pipeline extracts entities and relationships from source text chunks, partitions the resulting graph into communities using the Leiden algorithm, and summarizes each community. At query time, it generates partial answers from community summaries in parallel and synthesizes them into a final response. This differs from standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which retrieves local text chunks and fails on corpus-wide sensemaking questions.

The authors evaluated Graph RAG against naïve RAG and a map-reduce baseline that summarizes raw source texts directly. They used two datasets of approximately 1 million tokens and 125 LLM-generated sensemaking questions per dataset. An LLM-as-a-judge assessed answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness. Global approaches outperformed naïve RAG, with comprehensiveness win rates between 72% and 83%. Intermediate-level community summaries provided better comprehensiveness and diversity than source-text summarization while using 26–33% fewer context tokens. Root-level summaries reduced token usage by over 97% compared to source-text processing. Limitations include evaluation on only two specific datasets and question types, with no validation of fabrication rates or end-user utility.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RAG cannot answer corpus-wide sensemaking questions, so GraphRAG builds an entity graph with community summaries and outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers graph-based retrieval, hierarchical summaries and benchmarks oriented toward explicit fact retrieval rather than global questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects Leiden communities, summarizes them, and answers queries by map-reduce over summaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare six conditions on two corpora of about one million tokens, using generated global sensemaking questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Global GraphRAG conditions beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness at 72-83% win rates on podcast transcripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation covers only two corpora and lacks a fabrication-rate comparison, which the authors name as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Root-level community summaries give a data index that beats vector RAG and competes with other global methods at lower token cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extraction prompts, self-reflection gleaning, community detection, context window tests, an example comparison, and system prompts.

repos.title: Constraint Breeds Generalization: Temporal Dynamics as an Inductive Bias
repos.paper_summary: This paper argues that dissipative temporal dynamics, meaning phase-space contraction, act as an inductive bias that improves generalization in spiking neural networks (SNNs). Static features are converted into time series by a Duffing oscillator whose parameter δ sets the dynamics as expansive (δ<0), transition (δ≈0 to 2), or dissipative. Leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with leak β provide an architecture-level variant. On handwritten digits (64 features, 10 classes), SNNs trained in the transition regime generalize across a 12×12 matrix of encodings, while expansive-trained networks fail outside their training encoding. On CIFAR-10 patches, the transition regime yields localized, oriented receptive fields (structure score 0.206, versus 0.0541 for the best alternative in Table 1). Experiment 3 reports zero-shot transfer to unseen physical environments in reinforcement learning that beats baseline architectures. Limitations include fixed oscillator and fixed β parameters, and generality is checked only on a few alternative dynamical systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hypothesizes that dissipative temporal dynamics act as an inductive bias for generalization, tested at representational, structural, and behavioral levels.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Controls phase-space contraction through a single oscillator parameter δ for static inputs and neuron leak β for temporal inputs.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Argues the transition regime trades fit for stability; the authors flag fixed parameters and untested regime generality as limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Concludes that dissipative dynamics are an inductive bias, so generalization may depend on dynamical regime as much as on scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists oscillator equations and parameters, a dynamical indicator table, experiment details, Bayesian bound and gradient analyses, and extra figures.

repos.title: Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents
repos.paper_summary:
Agensh is a multi-agent harness that coordinates concurrent LLM workers without a central orchestrator. Each worker executes an asynchronous loop: gathering context, claiming sub-tasks, taking action, verifying results, and merging progress into a shared workspace. Coordination relies on three infrastructure components: a Git-based shared workspace for code integration, a message interface for peer communication, and a shared context board for reusable findings.

The paper evaluates Agensh on the five hardest ProgramBench tasks using GPT-5.6-sol (high) with a 6-hour budget. Scaling from 1 to 128 agents increases the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%, a 49% relative improvement. On the pandoc task, scaling to 1,024 agents raises the final test-pass rate from 33.89% to 55.06%. Larger organizations also reach comparable performance levels earlier; for instance, 128 agents exceed a 30% pass rate at 30 minutes, while single agents remain below this threshold for two hours. Limitations include reliance on specific underlying models and harnesses, and the need for staggered agent activation to manage scope contention in large-scale deployments.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agensh replaces a central orchestrator with self-organized workers, and scaling 1 to 128 agents raises mean test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Agent Organization Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Each worker repeats a five-step loop over a shared workspace, message interface and shared context, with no central orchestrator.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Multi-Agent Organization to 1,024 Agents
digest_headlines.headline: Mean test-pass rate rises with 8, 32 and 128 agents, and pandoc reaches 55.06% with 1,024 agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior harnesses keep task assignment under a fixed lead or trained orchestrator, while some tools coordinate workers through shared state.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agent count is proposed as a new scaling dimension, though every reported run uses one agent model.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the worker prompt, the event-driven runtime, the experiment configuration and the staggered agent launch schedule.

repos.title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation
repos.paper_summary: Hy-Nomas is an 8B-parameter video world model that generates interactive video from free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple turns. It is built on HunyuanVideo 1.5 and generates variable-length segments conditioned on the current input and cached history. Its main design choice is action-aware causal attention: structured captions describe persistent scene and subject context that stays visible to later segments, while timestamped action instructions are limited to their own time window. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and interaction history into structured conditions for each next segment. Training follows a multi-stage curriculum (causal generation, text interaction, camera control, training on model-generated histories), then diffusion distillation. Human evaluation is reported as favoring Hy-Nomas over existing world models, but the text provided does not include the scores. The paper notes that temporal causality does not establish physical causality, that robotics adaptation is shown only as an initial LoRA demonstration, and that retrieving past views does not update off-screen state, such as a clock that should keep running. Weights, code, and benchmarks are released.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hy-Nomas is an 8B interactive world model that follows free-form text and camera commands across multiple turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: Training videos are filtered, deduplicated, and annotated with camera trajectories and structured captions.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Action-aware causal attention limits each action to its own time window, and camera tokens condition each segment.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Infrastructure
digest_headlines.headline: Sequence parallelism, compute-balanced packing and masked attention kernels support training on sequences up to 360K tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training proceeds through causal, interaction and context curricula, then distillation from 100 to 4 steps per segment.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Inference
digest_headlines.headline: A vision-language Prompt Enhancer turns user requests into segment captions, and inference is optimized for a single device.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Human raters prefer Hy-Nomas over three interactive world models on most tasks, but Genie 3 leads on spatial memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Hy-Nomas is placed among video-based world models that add text and camera control to diffusion video generators.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Discussion names open challenges: response latency, action-grounded robotics, retrieval-based memory, and detailed caption quality.

digest_headlines.heading: Contributors
digest_headlines.headline: Contributors section lists core contributors, contributors, acknowledgments and leadership acknowledgments.
